plan.topic: What happens to your grocery cart on a GLP-1 medicine? The digital food-purchase study before and after GLP-1-based treatment (Diabetes Obes Metab, Oct 29, 2026)
plan.angle: If the DOM Oct 29 abstract can't be opened and confirmed, base the Short on the JAMA Network Open 2026 Danish receipt study. Opening line: 'After starting a GLP-1 medicine, people in a Danish study bought groceries with slightly fewer calories and less sugar per 100 grams, and a little more protein.' Then: observational; 293 starters versus 884 matched non-users; purchase receipts, not what people ate; 'linked to', not proof; the changes were modest. Title must name only the drugs the paper covered. If it reports only 'GLP-1 receptor agonists', use e.g. 'GLP-1 Medicines and Your Grocery Cart: What Changed #shorts'. Accuracy wins over the tirzepatide-first title rule here. Drop 'new' from the title. Keep the one biology line from L1's verified wording, the GI line, 'Not personal advice', the prescriber line, and the closing funnel line.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide and Your Grocery Cart: What a New Study Found #shorts
plan.why: Spin-off of L1. It's today's 20:00 Exp D funnel Short, driving viewers to the food noise long-form with a new, dated peer-reviewed fact. | fact-check: Same issue as L1: the 'Diabetes Obes Metab, Oct 29, 2026' digital food-purchase study couldn't be confirmed. The receipt study I could confirm is the Danish SMIL study in JAMA Network Open (early 2026): 293 GLP-1 RA starters versus 884 matched non-users, purchases logged through an app. That data is about nine months old, so don't call it 'new'. The title is risky: there's no evidence the Danish study covered tirzepatide users. Its period and setting suggest mostly semaglutide or other GLP-1 RAs. The brief's own rule says to put tirzepatide in the title only if the paper covered it. The changes were small, so the Short must say 'modest' and 'per 100 g of food bought'. It shouldn't imply people ate healthier or lost weight because of what they bought. Don't label foods 'bad'. Neutral wording like 'less ultra-processed' is fine if it's the paper's term.

factcheck.summary: The Short is accurate and safe to publish. I checked the Danish receipt study (Sørensen et al., JAMA Netw Open 2026;9(1):e2555449) in its PubMed record and in the full text on PMC, and every number matches. 293 people starting a GLP-1 medicine were matched 1:3 with 884 non-users on sex, age and 2017 income (by quartile). The starts were identified from 2019 to 2022, using supermarket receipts collected through a smartphone app over the 365 days before and after the first prescription. Per 100 g bought, calories fell by 2.1 kcal and sugar by 0.6 g, and protein rose by 0.3 g, so "slightly fewer", "less" and "a little more" are fair. The authors call the study cross-sectional, so "observational" and "linked, not proven" are correct, and "bought ≠ eaten" plus "modest" frame the limits well. The NHS semaglutide page confirms the wording "reducing your appetite and helping you to feel fuller for longer" and lists nausea, diarrhoea and constipation as common side effects. The safety lines are there, nothing gives dosing, switching or stopping advice, and the script is about 160 words. Two optional wording fixes are listed below; neither blocks publishing.

issues.claim: After starting a GLP-1 medicine, people in a Danish study bought groceries with slightly fewer calories…
issues.problem: The script doesn't name the comparison group until s3. A viewer could read s1 as a simple before-and-after change in starters, when the study compared them with matched non-users. The muted-viewer list also leaves out the comparison group.
issues.fix: Change list item 1 to: "Danish study: GLP-1 starters vs matched non-users". The narration can stay as it is, or change it to: "After starting a GLP-1 medicine, people in a Danish study bought groceries with slightly fewer calories and less sugar per one hundred grams of food bought, and a little more protein, compared with similar non-users."

issues.claim: Medicines like semaglutide can reduce appetite and help you feel fuller for longer.
issues.problem: The line is accurate (NHS) and the wording 'like' keeps it general. But the study didn't report which GLP-1 drugs people were taking, so the script shouldn't suggest the cart results are about semaglutide specifically.
issues.fix: Keep the line as written. Don't put a semaglutide or brand-specific hashtag or title on this Short, because the study didn't name the drugs.
